own_scenes.desc: La ciudad que en 1966 se convirtió en la meca internacional del pop. Bobby Jameson, de veinte años, en los márgenes de la industria (había grabado canciones tempranas de Jagger/Richards en Londres y se presentó al casting de los Monkees), grabó con miembros de los Leaves y el primer batería de Love «Vietnam» (Mira, octubre de 1965): órgano de película de terror, ritmo Bo Diddley y un aullido sin esperanza, el blues de un hombre blanco, retirado casi al instante. Detenido por drogas tras su primer LSD con Danny Hutton, se libró del reclutamiento al confesarlo en el examen. La adolescente Jan Smithers, habitual de Malibú y del Strip, decía a Newsweek que a veces quería gritar y golpear la almohada.

notes.chapter: Junio: I’ll Be Your Mirror: la Velvet Underground y la América de Warhol
notes.text: La Velvet y el EPI tocaron en mayo en The Trip, que cerró a los dos días por un pleito; quizá fueron una de las primeras víctimas de la campaña municipal y policial para limpiar el Strip de clubes y adolescentes. Sterling Morrison sintió que la Costa Oeste era una fuerza organizada que quería dominar el pop: en la radio sonaba «Monday Monday». Ese verano llegaban al Top 10 discos extraños y duros como «Along Comes Mary» de los Association o «Dirty Water» de los Standells.

notes.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje
notes.text: En 1966 el Strip, el tramo de Sunset entre Hollywood y Beverly Hills, era una «juventopía» de más de treinta y cinco clubes (Gazzari’s, London Fog, The Trip, Pandora’s Box) y un atasco permanente de adolescentes, promocionado por Shindig!, Where the Action Is y Shivaree; Canter’s era el punto de encuentro. Los Seeds de Sky Saxon (sin bajista, Daryl Hooper hacía los graves con el órgano) definieron la angustia adolescente y cantaron al ácido; Donovan retrató la escena en «The Trip». El LAPD acosaba a los chavales por merodear, mezclarse entre razas y drogas: el mapa de Freak Out! de los Mothers of Invention marcaba con explosiones atómicas los lugares de las redadas, y «Trouble Comin’ Every Day» de Frank Zappa fue la única canción de Los Ángeles sobre Watts. Mondo Hollywood captó la locura de neón y smog.

notes.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip
notes.text: El 12 de noviembre, cuatro días después de la victoria de Reagan, dos chicos de diecisiete años repartieron octavillas contra el maltrato policial a los jóvenes del Strip y entre mil y tres mil adolescentes se concentraron ante Pandora’s Box: un autobús asaltado, peleas con militares y titulares de «motín adolescente». Detrás había un pulso entre empresarios (los dueños de los clubes para menores contra los restaurantes de los hermanos Montgomery y el supervisor Ernest Debs) que exigían aplicar el toque de queda de las diez. El condado prohibió bailar a los menores en los clubes; los fines de semana siguientes la policía cargó contra cientos de chicos, detuvo a Peter Fonda («los chavales están hartos») y la industria musical (Jim Dickson, Elmer Valentine, David Anderle, Derek Taylor) creó CAFF, con «padres voluntarios» como testigos. El polvorín podía hacer de Watts «una merienda».

notes.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
notes.text: El 10 de diciembre RAMCON, de Al Mitchell, reunió a 2.000 manifestantes (clérigos, CAFF, Sonny & Cher); al dispersarse, la policía detuvo al director de la ACLU local y cargó con porras; el alcalde Yorty ordenó derribar Pandora’s Box. La industria lo convirtió en producto: los discos de explotación de los Leathercoated Minds (con J. J. Cale) y de Teddy & Darrel, «SOS» de Terry Randall, el «Sunset Symphony» grabado en la manifestación por Sonny Bono y, sobre todo, «For What It’s Worth» de Buffalo Springfield: una nueva clase de protesta, pausada y amenazante («Paranoia strikes deep»). Era una guerra generacional: «Old v. Young», según Derek Taylor.

refs.q: Bobby Jameson’s ‘Vietnam’ was a raw and brutal blast, a true cri de coeur from a young man facing the abyss.
refs.para: This fury can be found in an early protest record that captured a deeper emotional response to the possibility of being drawn into the conflict. Issued in mid-October 1965 on a small Los Angeles label, Mira – and almost instantly withdrawn because of its controversial approach – Bobby Jameson’s ‘Vietnam’ was a raw and brutal blast, a true cri de coeur from a young man facing the abyss.
refs.chapter: Marzo: The Ballad of the Green Berets: la guerra de Vietnam en Estados Unidos

refs.q: Shot in a murky half-light, the recording has the feeling of a blues session, and that’s what ‘Vietnam’ is: a white man’s blues.
refs.para: What they concocted was a vehement, swirling statement that captures the moment when the Vietnam war seemed to be spiralling out of control. Although it was quickly buried, footage of the song found its way into Robert Carl Cohen’s film Mondo Hollywood. It begins at the studio mixing desk: wearing extremely long hair and a three-day-old beard, Jameson dominates the screen, performing the song with unrestrained intensity, bellowing the lyrics from the bottom of his soul. Like Love, the band are interracial – a provocative statement in itself for Los Angeles, a highly segregated city. Shot in a murky half-light, the recording has the feeling of a blues session, and that’s what ‘Vietnam’ is: a white man’s blues.
refs.chapter: Marzo: The Ballad of the Green Berets: la guerra de Vietnam en Estados Unidos

refs.q: Domenic Priore speculates that the EPI were an early victim of the concerted city and police campaign to clear the Sunset Strip
refs.para: This incident has been presented as an example of West Coast hostility to the VU, but, quite apart from the actual dispute between the Trip’s operators, there was another possible factor. In his book Riot on Sunset Strip: Rock’n’Roll’s Last Stand in Hollywood, Domenic Priore speculates that the EPI were an early victim of the concerted city and police campaign to clear the Sunset Strip of clubs and teens, an operation that would explode later in the year.
refs.chapter: Junio: I’ll Be Your Mirror: la Velvet Underground y la América de Warhol

refs.q: With its endless suburbs, good weather and status as a major media centre, the extended Los Angeles area was the epicentre of this mood
refs.para: With its endless suburbs, good weather and status as a major media centre, the extended Los Angeles area was the epicentre of this mood, with the teen bands vying for space with already established acts like the Standells, Sons of Adam, and the Turtles, whose fifth single, the terrific, Stones-y ‘Outside Chance’, was released late that summer. All this activity was funnelled down one particular thoroughfare: the Sunset Strip.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: The Strip was saturated in drugs, and the West Coast musical references became ever more blatant
refs.para: The Strip was saturated in drugs, and the West Coast musical references became ever more blatant: ‘The Trip’, ‘Tripmaker’ and, most outrageous of all, the Other Half’s ‘Mr Pharmacist’, which pleaded with the drug dispenser for sackfuls of his produce. Drugs not only heightened and prolonged the teenage experience, they injected a new level of messianic address into the culture, as musicians and artists felt compelled to share the chimera of chemistry.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: The only LA group to sing about the Watts Riots were the Mothers of Invention.
refs.para: The only LA group to sing about the Watts Riots were the Mothers of Invention. Written by Frank Zappa, ‘Trouble Comin’ Every Day’ was a prolonged and troubled rumination on August 1965, full of anger at the obvious manipulations of the mass media and the intractable racial situation in America. The worst thing for Zappa was that the riots weren’t an isolated incident, but a perfect example of the violence and the stupidity of mid-1960s America.
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: Four days after Reagan’s election, a major disturbance erupted on Sunset Strip.
refs.para: Four days after Reagan’s election, a major disturbance erupted on Sunset Strip. There was a distinct feeling that a confrontation was inevitable, and the spark occurred when two seventeen-year-olds, fed up with what they saw as the oppressive LAPD presence on the Strip, printed up a few leaflets stating ‘that there would be a protest against the police on November the 12th at Pandora’s Box’. The complaint was of ‘Police mistreatment of youth on Sunset Blvd’, citing ‘Shackling of 14&15 year olds’ and ‘Arbitrary arrests of youths’.
refs.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip

refs.q: The Sunset Strip riots immediately became a litmus test of youth’s increasing assertiveness and the reactionary adult response.
refs.para: The Sunset Strip riots immediately became a litmus test of youth’s increasing assertiveness and the reactionary adult response. Writing in the Village Voice, Jules Siegel observed a connection between Mario Savio’s recent travails and ‘a thousand freaks demonstrating in the name of freedom on Sunset Strip Saturday night’: ‘in a very important way they were both different faces of the same force of change pumping through California and America in a marvellously powerful, however narrow stream – the force of the turned-on people’.
refs.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip

refs.q: ‘For What It’s Worth’ marked a new kind of protest.
refs.para: ‘For What It’s Worth’ marked a new kind of protest. Stills had lived in Costa Rica and El Salvador as a youth, and had seen how mass youth gatherings could effect regime change, if not revolution. America’s teenagers had learned well the lessons of the civil rights movement: as one young woman told Sonny Bono on the night of 10 December, ‘It’s history, because like maybe four years ago kids would have never done this, they never would have started rebelling for their own rights. Because they are people and they are right.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: The Sunset Strip riots, for all their self-dramatisation, were a pivotal event in American youth culture.
refs.para: The Sunset Strip riots, for all their self-dramatisation, were a pivotal event in American youth culture. To be sure, there was folly on both sides. The police were completely out of order, while there was a lot of provocation from the protestors, with their swastika placards. Sonny Bono’s tape recorder captured the burblings of one cynical young man: ‘Beautiful, it’s beautiful, it was great. I mean, you know if there’s nothing good on the Saturday night movies, you can’t beat it. Nothing like a good, clean-cut riot.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
